def-csm-frontier-mean-field-ensemble.finite_checks_disposition: No computation is applicable to a definition; the complete finite-alphabet state spaces, product weights, tilt, and shell conventions appear in the interface.
def-csm-frontier-mean-field-ensemble.definition_interface:
Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

derivations.claim: Since $K$ is compact, $F$ is bounded above and below. Since $I$ is not identically $+\infty$, choose $x_0\in K$ with $I(x_0)<+\infty$. Therefore $F(x_0)-I(x_0)\leq c\leq\sup_K F<+\infty$, so $c$ is finite. The integrand $e^{nF}$ is bounded above and bounded below by the positive constant $e^{n\inf_KF}$, and $\mu_n$ is a probability measure, hence $0<Z_n<+\infty$ and $\nu_n^F$ is a probability measure.

Let $G\subseteq K$ be open, let $x\in G$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, and let $\varepsilon>0$. Continuity of $F$ gives an open neighborhood $U$ with $x\in U\subseteq G$ and $F(y)>F(x)-\varepsilon$ for every $y\in U$. Hence $\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq e^{n(F(x)-\varepsilon)}\mu_n(U)$. By [A1], the logarithm of this integral divided by $n$ has liminf at least $F(x)-\varepsilon-\inf_U I\geq F(x)-\varepsilon-I(x)$. Taking the supremum over finite-rate $x\in G$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the open-set integral lower bound $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln\int_G e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\geq\sup_{x\in G}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $C\subseteq K$ be closed. For any $x\in C$ with $I(x)<+\infty$, lower semicontinuity of $I$ and continuity of $F$ give an open neighborhood $V_x$ on which $F\leq F(x)+\varepsilon$ and $I\geq I(x)-\varepsilon$; choose a ball $U_x$ centered at $x$ with $\overline U_x\subseteq V_x$. If $I(x)=+\infty$, choose $M>\sup_KF-c+1$, use lower semicontinuity to choose $V_x$ with $I>M$, and again choose such a ball. Compactness of $C$ supplies a finite cover by these $U_x$; put $C_j:=C\cap\overline U_{x_j}$ for its closed pieces. For finite-rate centers, $\sup_{C_j}F-\inf_{C_j}I\leq F(x_j)-I(x_j)+2\varepsilon\leq c+2\varepsilon$; for infinite-rate centers, the same expression is at most $\sup_KF-M<c-1$. The integral over $C$ is bounded by the finite sum $\sum_j e^{n\sup_{C_j}F}\mu_n(C_j)$. Applying [A1] to each closed $C_j$ and using that a finite sum has logarithmic limsup no greater than its largest summand gives $\limsup_n n^{-1}\ln\int_C e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq c+2\varepsilon$. Letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ proves the closed-set integral upper bound $\limsup_n n^{-1}\ln\int_C e^{nF}\,d\mu_n\leq\sup_{x\in C}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Taking $G=K$ in step 1.2 and $C=K$ in step 1.3 gives $\liminf_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\geq c$ and $\limsup_n n^{-1}\ln Z_n\leq c$, proving the log-Laplace limit. The function $I_F=I-F+c$ is lower semicontinuous, is nonnegative by the definition of $c$, and has compact sublevel sets because those sets are closed in compact $K$. Also $F-I$ is upper semicontinuous, bounded above by $\sup_KF$, and finite at the point chosen in step 1.1; hence it attains the finite supremum $c$ on compact $K$. Equality $I_F(x)=0$ holds exactly when $F(x)-I(x)=c$, so its nonempty zero set is precisely the stated maximizing set.

For open $G\subseteq K$, apply the open-set integral lower bound from step 1.2 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_G(F-I)-c=-\inf_G I_F$, this is the LDP lower bound for $\nu_n^F$.

For closed $C\subseteq K$, apply the closed-set integral upper bound from step 1.3 and subtract the log-normalizer limit in step 2.1. Since $\sup_C(F-I)-c=-\inf_C I_F$, this is the LDP upper bound for $\nu_n^F$.

Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite, let $p$ be a probability vector on $\mathcal A$, and set $S:=\operatorname{supp}(p)=\{a\in\mathcal A:p(a)>0\}$. Then $S$ is finite nonempty and $p(a)>0$ on $S$. For each $n\ge1$, use the finite product law $p^{\otimes n}$ from [[def-it-finite-alphabet-product-law]] and [[lem-it-finite-product-law-is-iid]] on $\mathcal A^n$, and let $X_1^{(n)},\ldots,X_n^{(n)}$ be its coordinate maps. Let $\widehat P_n$ be the empirical type of this coordinate word, viewed as a $\Delta(\mathcal A)$-valued map. Identify the support simplex
$$\Delta(S):=\{q\in[0,1]^S:\sum_{a\in S}q(a)=1\}$$
with the face of $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ whose coordinates outside $S$ vanish. Then $\widehat P_n\in\Delta(S)$ almost surely under $p^{\otimes n}$. For any set $\Gamma\subseteq\Delta(S)$, let $\Gamma^\circ$ and $\overline\Gamma$ denote its interior and closure in the relative topology induced by $\|\cdot\|_1$.
With $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$,
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\ge-\inf_{q\in\Gamma^\circ}D(q\|p),$$
and
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le-\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p).$$
For every $n\ge1$ the finite upper bound
$$p^{\otimes n}(\widehat P_n\in\Gamma)\le(n+1)^{|S|-1}\exp\!\left(-n\inf_{q\in\overline\Gamma}D(q\|p)\right)$$
also holds. If the two infima agree, the limit exists and equals their negative common value. Equivalently, when $S\ne\mathcal A$, one may restrict the product sample space to $S^n$ without changing these event probabilities, since every word outside $S^n$ has zero product mass.

Let $(K,d_K)$ be a nonempty compact metric space and let $(\mu_n)_{n\geq1}$ be Borel probability measures on $K$. Let $I:K\to[0,+\infty]$ be lower semicontinuous and not identically $+\infty$. Assume the speed-$n$ large-deviation bounds
$$\liminf_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(G)\geq-\inf_{x\in G}I(x)\quad\text{for every open }G\subseteq K,$$
$$\limsup_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln\mu_n(C)\leq-\inf_{x\in C}I(x)\quad\text{for every closed }C\subseteq K,$$
with $\inf\varnothing=+\infty$ and $\ln0=-\infty$. Let $F:K\to\mathbb R$ be continuous and put
$$Z_n:=\int_K e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x),\qquad c:=\sup_{x\in K}\bigl(F(x)-I(x)\bigr).$$
For Borel $B\subseteq K$, define the normalized exponential tilt
$$\nu_n^F(B):=Z_n^{-1}\int_B e^{nF(x)}\,d\mu_n(x).$$
Then $Z_n$ is finite and positive,
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln Z_n=c,$$
and $(\nu_n^F)$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with the good rate function $I_F(x):=I(x)-F(x)+c$. Its zero set is precisely $\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in K}(F(x)-I(x))$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and let $p$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$. Then $q\mapsto D(q\|p)$ is finite and continuous on the probability simplex $\Delta(\mathcal A)$.

For probability vectors $p=(p_i)_{i\in I}$ and $q=(q_i)_{i\in I}$ on a finite nonempty set $I$, define

$$D(p\|q):=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\sum_{i:p_i>0}p_i\ln\frac{p_i}{q_i},&p_i>0\Rightarrow q_i>0,\\+\infty,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Then $D(p\|q)\ge0$, and $D(p\|q)=0$ if and only if $p=q$.

derivations.claim: By [F4], $q\mapsto D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)$ is continuous on compact $\Delta(\mathcal A)$, so it attains a finite minimum $m_\beta$. The rate $D$ is nonnegative by [F5]. The empirical macrostate law under $p^{\otimes n}$ has rate $D(q\|p)$ by [F2]. For every Borel $B\subseteq\Delta(\mathcal A)$, the canonical macrostate probability is exactly $$p_{n,\beta}(L_n\in B)=\frac{\int_B e^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)}{\int_{\Delta(\mathcal A)} e^{-n\beta h(q)}\,d\mu_n(q)},$$ where $\mu_n$ is the base law of $L_n$; this follows by summing the word weights in [F1] over the fiber $L_n^{-1}(B)$. Thus it is the tilt in [F3] with $F=-\beta h$, and its rate is $D+\beta h-m_\beta$. Its zero set is $\mathcal M_\beta$. Every open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_\beta$ has closed complement on which this continuous rate has a strictly positive minimum, so the LDP upper bound makes the canonical macrostate probability of that complement exponentially small.

The fiber $H_u:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u\}$ is nonempty and compact because $u$ is in the range of continuous $h$. By [F4], $D$ attains its finite minimum $d(u)$ on $H_u$, so $\mathcal M_u$ is nonempty. For fixed $\delta>0$, put $B_\delta:=\{q:|h(q)-u|<\delta\}$; it is open and contains $H_u$. By [F2], $$-\inf_{B_\delta}D\leq\liminf_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq\limsup_n\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}(L_n\in B_\delta)\leq-\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D.$$ For each matching radius $\delta_j$ in the Statement the two infima agree, so the inner limit exists and equals their negative common value. The lower bound is finite because $B_{\delta_j}$ contains a finite-rate point of $H_u$; hence the conditioning event has positive probability for all sufficiently large $n$.

Let $q\in\mathcal M_\beta$ and put $u=h(q)$. If $r\in H_u$, then $D(r)+\beta u\geq D(q)+\beta u$, so $q\in\mathcal M_u$ and $D(q)=d(u)$. For any $v$ in the energy range, minimizing over $H_v$ gives $d(v)+\beta v\geq d(u)+\beta u$, equivalently $s(v)-\beta v\leq s(u)-\beta u$. Thus $u$ maximizes the stated entropy-minus-energy expression.

Write $d_\delta:=\inf_{\overline B_\delta}D$ for any $\delta>0$; since $H_u\subseteq\overline B_\delta$, $d_\delta\leq d(u)$. Fix $\varepsilon>0$ and let $K_\varepsilon:=\{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):D(q\|p)\leq d(u)-\varepsilon\}$. By [F4], this set is compact; it is disjoint from $H_u$ by the definition of $d(u)$. Thus its compact image $h(K_\varepsilon)$ does not contain $u$ and has positive distance from $u$ (if it is empty, the conclusion is immediate). For every sufficiently small $\delta$, the closed shell $\overline B_\delta$ misses $K_\varepsilon$, so $d_\delta\geq d(u)-\varepsilon$. Together with $d_\delta\leq d(u)$, this proves $d_\delta\to d(u)$ as $\delta\downarrow0$, in particular along the matching sequence $\delta_j$. Step 1.2 now gives the iterated shell limit $-d(u)=s(u)$.

Let $U$ be an open neighborhood of $\mathcal M_u$ and put $C:=\Delta(\mathcal A)\setminus U$. If $C\cap H_u$ is empty, compactness makes $h(C)$ a compact set separated from $u$, so sufficiently small shells miss $C$. Otherwise, continuity of $D$ on compact $C\cap H_u$ gives $d_C:=\min_{C\cap H_u}D>d(u)$, since $C$ contains no constrained minimizer. Choose $0<\eta<d_C-d(u)$ and set $K:=\{q\in C:D(q)\leq d(u)+\eta\}$; this is compact and disjoint from $H_u$, so $h(K)$ is separated from $u$. Hence for all sufficiently small $\delta$, $\inf_{C\cap\overline B_\delta}D\geq d(u)+\eta$. For every sufficiently small matching radius $\delta_j$, we also have $d_{\delta_j}<d(u)+\eta/2$. The LDP upper bound [F2] on the closed set $\overline{C\cap B_{\delta_j}}\subseteq C\cap\overline B_{\delta_j}$ bounds the numerator's logarithmic limsup exponent by $-d(u)-\eta$. By step 1.2 the denominator's logarithmic limit exponent is $-d_{\delta_j}$, so subtracting gives a conditional logarithmic limsup at most $d_{\delta_j}-d(u)-\eta<-\eta/2$. Thus for every sufficiently large $j$ the conditional probability tends to zero exponentially as $n\to\infty$, which gives the asserted iterated concentration limit.

Conversely, let $u$ maximize $s(v)-\beta v$ and let $q\in\mathcal M_u$. For any $r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, put $v=h(r)$. Then $D(r)+\beta v\geq d(v)+\beta v\geq d(u)+\beta u=D(q)+\beta u$, so $q\in\mathcal M_\beta$. This proves both the equality of energy sets and the macrostate criterion. Rearranging $s(v)-\beta v\leq s(u)-\beta u$ gives exactly $s(v)\leq s(u)+\beta(v-u)$; hence the criterion is the stated upper-supporting-line condition, with no formal inverse-transform assumption.

boundaries.evidence: The Statement restricts u to h(Δ(A)), so every constrained fiber H_u is nonempty; step 1.2 records this.
Full support makes D finite and continuous even at simplex coordinates q(a)=0 by F4 and step 1.2.
For a one-letter alphabet Δ(A) is a singleton, and the compact-minimum and variational identities in steps 1.1–4.1 remain valid.
If h is constant, its range is a one-point energy set; steps 1.3 and 4.1 still apply.
For endpoint energies in h(Δ(A)), the fiber remains compact and nonempty; step 1.2 uses no interior-energy assumption.
Steps 1.1 and 1.2 obtain minima from compactness; steps 2.1–3.1 use compact image separation, with no choice axiom.
Step 1.3 proves a canonical q is constrained-minimizing and its energy maximizes s(v)-βv.
Step 4.1 proves every constrained minimizer at a maximizing energy is canonical.

finite_checks.check: Use A={0,1}, p=(r,1-r) with 0<r<1, h(q)=q(0), and β=0.
finite_checks.result: Each energy fiber is the single q=(u,1-u), s(u)=-D(q||p), and D≥0 with equality only at u=r; the canonical and supported energy sets are both {r}.
finite_checks.verifies: The finite-alphabet variational and upper-supporting-line equivalence in steps 1.1–4.1.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with

derivations.claim: Write $q(+1)=(1+m)/2$ and $q(-1)=(1-m)/2$. Substituting into [F1] with $p(+1)=p(-1)=1/2$ gives $$D(q\|p)=\frac{1+m}{2}\ln(1+m)+\frac{1-m}{2}\ln(1-m),$$ with endpoint terms omitted when their coefficient is zero. Since $h(q)=-Jm^2/2$, the canonical objective $D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)$ is exactly $\Phi_\beta(m)$. It is continuous on $[-1,1]$ using $0\ln0=0$ and even in $m$.

For $|m|<1$ define $a(m):=\operatorname{atanh}(m):=\tfrac12\ln\frac{1+m}{1-m}$. By [F3]–[F5] and direct differentiation, $$a'(m)=\frac1{1-m^2},\qquad \Phi_\beta'(m)=a(m)-\beta Jm.$$ For $0<m<1$ put $g(m):=a(m)/m$ and define $r:[0,1)\to\mathbb R$ by $r(m):=m/(1-m^2)-a(m)$. Then $g'(m)=r(m)/m^2$, $r(0)=0$, and $r'(m)=2m^2/(1-m^2)^2>0$ for $0<m<1$. The mean value theorem [F6] applies to $r$ on $[0,m]$ because $r$ is continuous there and differentiable on $(0,m)$; it gives $r(m)>0$, hence $g'(m)>0$.

The same theorem [F6] applied to $a$ on $[0,m]$ gives $g(m)=a'(c_m)$ for some $c_m\in(0,m)$; as $m\downarrow0$, $c_m\downarrow0$ and $a'(c_m)\to1$, so $\lim_{m\downarrow0}g(m)=1$. As $m\uparrow1$, $(1+m)/(1-m)\to+\infty$, and the increasing onto logarithm [F3] gives $a(m)\to+\infty$, hence $g(m)\to+\infty$. Thus $g$ is continuous, strictly increasing from limiting value $1$ to $+\infty$ on $(0,1)$.

If $\beta J\leq1$, then for $0<m<1$, $\Phi_\beta'(m)=m(g(m)-\beta J)>0$ by step 2.1. The mean value theorem [F6] on each subinterval of $[0,1]$ makes $\Phi_\beta$ strictly increasing there; continuity includes the endpoint $m=1$. Evenness then shows $\Phi_\beta(m)>\Phi_\beta(0)$ for every $m\neq0$, so $0$ is the unique global minimizer.

If $\beta J>1$, the limits in step 2.1 give $a,b$ with $0<a<b<1$, $g(a)<\beta J<g(b)$. Continuity of $g$ on $[a,b]$ and the intermediate value theorem [F7] give an $m_\beta\in(a,b)$ with $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$; strict increase of $g$ makes it unique on $(0,1)$. The derivative formula in step 1.2 is negative for $0<m<m_\beta$ and positive for $m_\beta<m<1$. By [F6], $\Phi_\beta$ strictly decreases on $[0,m_\beta]$ and strictly increases on $[m_\beta,1]$, including the endpoint by continuity. Evenness proves that the only global minimizers on $[-1,1]$ are $\pm m_\beta$; in particular the stationary point $m=0$ is not a minimizer.

The equation $g(m_\beta)=\beta J$ is $\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)=\beta Jm_\beta$. If $r=(1+m_\beta)/(1-m_\beta)$, then $e^{2\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta)}=e^{\ln r}=r$ by [F3], so the stated formula for $\tanh$ gives $\tanh(\operatorname{atanh}(m_\beta))=(r-1)/(r+1)=m_\beta$. Hence $m_\beta=\tanh(\beta Jm_\beta)$. Conversely, any $m\in(0,1)$ solving this fixed-point equation yields $e^{2\beta Jm}=(1+m)/(1-m)$ by rearrangement of the stated $\tanh$ formula; applying $\ln$ and [F3] gives $g(m)=\beta J$. Strict increase of $g$ therefore proves uniqueness of the positive fixed point. By [F2], the global minimizers just classified are exactly the canonical equilibrium magnetizations.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a finite nonempty alphabet, let $p=(p(a))_{a\in\mathcal A}$ be a probability vector with $p(a)>0$ for every $a$, and write
$$\Delta(\mathcal A):=\left\{q\in[0,1]^{\mathcal A}:\sum_{a\in\mathcal A}q(a)=1\right\}$$
with its $\ell^1$ topology. For each integer $n\geq1$, the configuration space is $\Omega_n:=\mathcal A^n$ with the full power-set $\sigma$-algebra. Its reference probability is the product law $p^{\otimes n}$, which gives the word $x^n=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ mass $\prod_{i=1}^n p(x_i)$. The empirical macrostate is the probability vector
$$L_n(x^n)(a):=\frac1n\#\{i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}:x_i=a\},\qquad a\in\mathcal A.$$
Thus $L_n$ is the empirical type defined by the finite-alphabet supplier.

For a continuous function $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ and a real parameter $\beta$, define the finite canonical normalizer and word law by
$$Z_{n,\beta}:=\sum_{x^n\in\Omega_n}p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))},\qquad p_{n,\beta}(x^n):=\frac{p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}}{Z_{n,\beta}}.$$
The normalizer is finite and positive because the sum is finite and every summand is finite and positive. The canonical macrostate law is the pushforward $p_{n,\beta}\circ L_n^{-1}$.

For $q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)$, set
$$D(q\|p):=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln\frac{q(a)}{p(a)},$$
omitting zero-mass terms, as in the finite relative-entropy convention. For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, define the constrained cost, entropy, canonical variational set, and constrained variational set by
$$d(u):=\inf_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p),\qquad s(u):=-d(u),$$
$$\mathcal M_\beta:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)\bigr],\qquad \mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A):h(q)=u}D(q\|p).$$
For $\delta>0$, the microcanonical shell event is $E_{n,\delta,u}:=\{x^n:|h(L_n(x^n))-u|<\delta\}$. Whenever $p^{\otimes n}(E_{n,\delta,u})>0$, its microcanonical shell law is the conditional probability $p^{\otimes n}(\,\cdot\mid E_{n,\delta,u})$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be finite and nonempty, let $p(a)>0$ for every $a\in\mathcal A$, and let $h:\Delta(\mathcal A)\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, where $\Delta(\mathcal A)$ is the probability simplex with its $\ell^1$ topology. Let $L_n$ be the empirical probability vector of an $n$-word drawn from $p^{\otimes n}$, and use $D(q\|p)=\sum_{a:q(a)>0}q(a)\ln(q(a)/p(a))$ with zero-mass terms omitted. For $\beta\in\mathbb R$, the canonical word law weights $x^n$ proportionally to $p^{\otimes n}(x^n)e^{-n\beta h(L_n(x^n))}$.

The canonical macrostate law of $L_n$ satisfies a speed-$n$ large-deviation principle with rate
$$R_\beta(q)=D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)-m_\beta,\qquad m_\beta:=\min_{r\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}\bigl[D(r\|p)+\beta h(r)\bigr].$$
Thus its canonical equilibrium macrostate set is $\mathcal M_\beta=\operatorname*{argmin}_{q\in\Delta(\mathcal A)}[D(q\|p)+\beta h(q)]$.

For $u\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))$, let $d(u):=\min_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$, $s(u):=-d(u)$, and $\mathcal M_u:=\operatorname*{argmin}_{h(q)=u}D(q\|p)$. If there is a sequence $\delta_j\downarrow0$ for which
$$\inf_{|h(q)-u|<\delta_j}D(q\|p)=\inf_{|h(q)-u|\leq\delta_j}D(q\|p)\quad\text{for every }j,$$
then the iterated microcanonical shell limit exists and is
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac1n\ln p^{\otimes n}\!\left(|h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=s(u).$$
In the same iterated limit, for every open neighborhood $U$ of $\mathcal M_u$,
$$\lim_{j\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}p^{\otimes n}\!\left(L_n\notin U\mid |h(L_n)-u|<\delta_j\right)=0.$$
Finally,
$$h(\mathcal M_\beta)=\operatorname*{argmax}_{v\in h(\Delta(\mathcal A))}\bigl[s(v)-\beta v\bigr],$$
and a macrostate $q$ is canonical at $\beta$ exactly when $q\in\mathcal M_{h(q)}$ and $h(q)$ maximizes $s(v)-\beta v$. Equivalently, $u$ is a canonical energy at $\beta$ exactly when $v\mapsto s(u)+\beta(v-u)$ is an upper supporting affine function for $s$ on the whole energy range. An energy with no upper supporting line for any slope is not realized by a canonical ensemble.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because The exponential is a continuous bijection from $\mathbb{R}$ onto $(0,\infty)$ states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

Thus $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is the inverse function of $\exp$. In particular, $\log(\exp y)=y$ for every $y\in\mathbb R$ and $\exp(\log x)=x$ for every $x>0$.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,
$$\log(xy)=\log x+\log y,\qquad \log(x/y)=\log x-\log y,\qquad \log(1/x)=-\log x.$$
Also $\log 1=0$.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

derivations.claim: If $h(q)=u>0$, then $q(1)=u^4$ and $q(0)=1-u^4$, so the constraint fiber is a singleton. The relative-entropy formula in [F1] gives $D(q\|p)=u^4\ln(2u^4)+(1-u^4)\ln(2(1-u^4))=\ln2-H_2(u^4)$; hence $s(u)=H_2(u^4)-\ln2$.
For $0<u<1$, [F4]–[F5] give $H_2'(x)=\ln((1-x)/x)$ and therefore $s'(u)=4u^3\ln((1-u^4)/u^4)$. Differentiating once more yields $s''(u)=u^2 B(u)$, where $B(u):=12\ln((1-u^4)/u^4)-16/(1-u^4)$.

On $0<u\leq1/9$, $R(u):=(1-u^4)/u^4=u^{-4}-1$ decreases and $1/(1-u^4)$ increases, so $B(u)$ decreases. At $u=1/9$, $R(u)=6560$ and $B(1/9)=12\ln6560-16\cdot6561/6560$. Since $6560>16$, [F3] gives $\ln6560>\ln16=4\ln2$; and [F4] gives $\ln2=\int_1^2dt/t>1/2$ because $1/t\geq1/2$ on $[1,2]$ with strict inequality on $[1,2)$. Thus $12\ln6560>24$. Also $16\cdot6561/6560<17$ by integer multiplication, so $B(1/9)>7$ and $B(u)>0$ throughout $(0,1/9]$. In particular $s''(u)>0$ on that interval. By applying [F6] first to $s'$ and then to $s$, positive second derivative makes $s'$ strictly increasing and every interior chord lie strictly above the graph; hence $s$ is strictly convex on $(0,1/9)$.

Fix $u\in(0,1/10]$ and choose $t>0$ so that $0<u-t<u+t<1/9$, possible because $1/10<1/9$. Strict convexity from step 3.1 gives $s(u-t)+s(u+t)>2s(u)$. If an upper supporting line with slope $\beta$ existed at $u$, its inequalities at $u-t$ and $u+t$ would instead give $s(u-t)+s(u+t)\leq[s(u)-\beta t]+[s(u)+\beta t]=2s(u)$, a contradiction. By [F2], no such energy is canonical for any real $\beta$.
